<reason>PRO (Side B) won by keeping the comparison anchored to the motion as written—"permit," not mandate—and by repeatedly converting CON's own history and admissions into support. CON's Zurich account conceded rooms were part of the package that worked; CON's "police cannot hold a perimeter" admission undercut its later reliance on "enforced dispersal"; and CON's answer to B's pressure question (a nurse with naloxone riding with outreach) conceded the core mechanism, which B crystallized as "a supervised consumption site with the roof torn off." CON's strongest live routes—limited coverage and the fixed-address/magnet risk in weakly policed Latin American cities—were pointed and CON's pressure questions were sharp, but B answered them directly (sites sit inside the open scene where deaths cluster; the crowd is already fixed; prohibition funds none of the other legs), while CON's replies leaned on unsupported assertion ("same bodies rearranged," "draws two more into daily use"). Both sides used plausible background knowledge without fake precision. CON was competent and memorable, but B made the decision easier and finished with the cleaner weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.4–B4.5 and B5.1–B5.3: B combined CON's "poor city picks the cheapest leg" and "police cannot hold a perimeter" admissions to show CON's alternative (dispersal) is impossible by CON's own account, then reframed CON's outreach-nurse alternative as the same mechanism minus the roof, leaving CON quarreling only about the building.</best_rebuttal>
